chapter_title: Basic Electronics for Arduino: Voltage, Current, Resistance, and Breadboards
chapter_summary:
Arduino projects combine software with electronics, so a basic understanding of electricity is necessary. Electricity can be understood using a water analogy. Voltage is like water pressure: it is the force that pushes electrons through a circuit. Current is like the flow rate: it is the amount of charge passing through a point per second. Resistance is like a narrow section of pipe: it limits how much current can flow.

Ohm's Law relates these three quantities: V = I × R, where V is voltage in volts, I is current in amps, and R is resistance in ohms. This law is essential for choosing resistors. For example, if you connect a red LED to the 5V output of an Arduino pin, the LED might try to draw too much current and burn out. By adding a 220-ohm resistor, you limit the current to a safe value. Using Ohm's Law, I = V / R = (5V - 2V) / 220Ω ≈ 13.6 milliamps, which is within the safe range for both the LED and the Arduino pin.

A breadboard is a reusable platform for building circuits without soldering. It has a grid of holes connected internally by metal clips. The holes along the long edges, usually marked with red and blue lines, are power rails. All holes in a single rail are connected together. The holes in the middle section are arranged in short rows of five, with each row connected internally but separated by a central groove. This groove matches the width of integrated circuits and other components. Components plug into the breadboard, and jumper wires connect them to the Arduino pins and power rails.

When building a circuit, always turn off or disconnect power before making changes. Use the correct color convention for jumper wires: red for positive power, black or blue for ground, and other colors for signals. Check that LED polarity is correct: the longer leg is the anode (positive) and the shorter leg is the cathode (negative). If connected backwards, the LED will not light. Resistors are not polarized, so they can be inserted either way.

Common mistakes include connecting a component directly across 5V and GND without a resistor, which creates a short circuit; exceeding the current limit of an Arduino pin; and confusing rows on the breadboard. Always verify your wiring against a diagram before applying power, and use the current-limiting resistor whenever an LED is involved.

screens.subtitle: Voltage, current, resistance, and how to wire an LED on a breadboard

narration.text: In this lesson we'll connect familiar ideas about water and pipes to the behavior of electricity so you can reason about simple Arduino circuits. You will learn what voltage, current, and resistance mean, how they relate through Ohm's Law, and how to choose a current-limiting resistor for an LED. You'll also learn how a breadboard is organized, why LED polarity matters, and the simple safety habits that protect your components and your Arduino. A concrete example will walk you through sizing a resistor for a red LED on a five-volt pin and then building the LED blink circuit on a breadboard. Throughout, I will point out common mistakes beginners make, such as connecting components directly between five volts and ground, and how to avoid them. By the end of this chapter you'll be able to calculate the expected current, place parts correctly on a breadboard, check LED orientation, and reliably test an external LED with the Blink sketch. Keep these practical rules in mind as we move into step-by-step wiring and experiments.

screens.title: Voltage, current, and resistance — the water analogy
screens.subtitle: A mental model to reason about circuits

narration.text: A helpful mental model for electricity is water moving through pipes. Voltage is like the pressure pushing water through a pipe. It doesn’t flow by itself but provides the force that makes charges move. Current is the flow rate: how much water passes a point each second. In electronics it measures charge per second in amps. Resistance is the constriction in the pipe that limits how much water can flow for a given pressure. If you increase resistance, current goes down for the same voltage. This analogy helps when you assemble circuits: higher voltage can push more current through the same resistor, smaller resistance allows more current, and a bad connection behaves like a partial blockage. Use this model to predict what happens when you add more components in series or parallel. A common misconception is to treat voltage as the same as current; they are different properties. Voltage tells you how strongly the circuit can push, current tells you how much is actually moving, and resistance controls the relationship. Practice saying the three definitions aloud while looking at a simple circuit and you will retain the connection between the words and the physical behavior.

Module 2 › Chapter 1.4 › Voltage & Flow
Definition

Water analogy for electricity

Use pressure, flow, and constriction to reason about voltage, current, and resistance in circuits. This helps predict how parts interact without complex math at first.

Voltage (pressure)
Force that pushes electrons; measured in volts.
Current (flow)
Rate of charge movement; measured in amps.
Resistance (constriction)
Limits current for a given voltage; measured in ohms.
Key Takeaway

The analogy helps you estimate behavior: raising pressure or lowering constriction increases flow.

Concrete example
Imagine a 5V source and a narrow resistor. The resistor restricts current; if you reduce resistance the current rises. This intuition prepares you to use Ohm's Law precisely in the next screen.
Common misconception
Voltage is not the same as current. Saying 'more voltage means more current' is incomplete — current depends on resistance as well.
Try this
Before you wire anything, say the analogy out loud: identify pressure, flow, and constriction in the planned circuit. This builds intuitive checks for later calculations.

screens.title: Ohm's Law: V = I × R
screens.subtitle: Relate voltage, current, and resistance with units and rearrangements

narration.text: Ohm's Law states that voltage equals current times resistance, V equals I times R. This simple equation links the three quantities and gives you the ability to compute whichever value is missing. When working with an LED and Arduino, you'll often know the supply voltage and the LED forward voltage, and you want to find the resistor value that keeps current within a safe range. Rearranged, I equals V divided by R gives current for a known resistor. Alternatively, R equals V divided by I tells you the resistor value to achieve a target current. Keep units straight: volts, amps, and ohms. In small-signal circuits we usually measure current in milliamps; converting units before computing avoids mistakes. A frequent beginner error is neglecting to subtract the LED forward voltage from the supply before applying Ohm's Law. For example, with five volts supply and a two-volt LED drop, use three volts as the voltage across the resistor. Practicing these rearrangements with example numbers will make resistor selection second nature. Ohm's Law: V = I × R means use v = i × r and its rearrangements to compute current or resistor values; remember to account for component voltage drops.. In practical terms, relate voltage, current, and resistance with units and rearrangements. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.4 › Ohm's Law
Definition

V = I × R

Learn the rearrangements and unit consistency to compute current or resistance accurately in LED circuits.

I = V / R
Current in amps when voltage across the resistor and resistance are known.
R = V / I
Choose resistor value to obtain a target current.
Worked example
Suppose a 5V pin drives a red LED with a 2V forward drop and you want safe LED current. The resistor sees 3V. For a 220-ohm resistor, current is I = 3V / 220Ω ≈ 0.0136 A, or 13.6 milliamps. This is within a typical safe range for an LED and an Arduino output pin.
Common mistake
Do not use the supply voltage directly when an LED or other device has a significant forward voltage. Subtract the device drop first before computing resistor current.

screens.title: Sizing a resistor for an LED — step by step
screens.subtitle: A clear numerical workflow you can repeat

narration.text: When sizing a resistor for an LED there is a short repeatable process to follow. Step one: identify the supply voltage and the LED forward voltage from the component datasheet or typical values; for a red LED that is often around two volts. Step two: compute the voltage across the resistor by subtracting the LED forward voltage from the supply voltage. Step three: choose a target current that is safe for both the LED and the Arduino pin, often between ten and twenty milliamps for simple LEDs. Step four: use R equals V divided by I to compute the needed resistance, making sure to use amps when computing. Step five: pick the nearest standard resistor value equal to or larger than the computed value, because a higher resistor reduces current and is safer. A common practical check is to start with 220 ohms and observe brightness; substituting a 1k resistor reduces brightness noticeably. This workflow minimizes errors and gives you predictable brightness and current draw for your prototype circuits. Sizing a resistor for an LED — step by step means identify voltages, pick target current, compute r = vdrop / i, then choose the nearest equal or larger resistor value.. In practical terms, a clear numerical workflow you can repeat. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Repeatable workflow
keyIdea.text: Identify voltages, pick target current, compute R = Vdrop / I, then choose the nearest equal or larger resistor value.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.4 › Resistor sizing
Process

Five steps to choose a resistor

1
Know supply and LED forward voltage.
2
Compute resistor voltage: Vdrop = Vsupply − Vled.
3
Choose a target current (e.g., 10–20 mA).
4
Compute R = Vdrop / I (use amps).
5
Pick the nearest equal or larger standard resistor.
Example
With 5V supply and a 2V LED drop, Vdrop is 3V. For 15 mA target current, R = 3V / 0.015 A = 200 ohms. Choose 220 ohms as the nearest common value.
Try it
Start with 220 ohms, observe brightness, then swap to 1k to see the brightness decrease, confirming the current dropped.

screens.title: LEDs: polarity and forward voltage
screens.subtitle: Why LED orientation and voltage drop matter

narration.text: Light-emitting diodes are polarized components: they conduct current and emit light only when the anode is more positive than the cathode. The longer leg of a through-hole LED is the anode or positive side, and the shorter leg is the cathode or negative side. If you connect an LED backwards it will not light, though in most low-voltage experiments it will not be damaged if current is limited. LEDs also have a forward voltage: the voltage they drop when conducting, which varies by color. A red LED typically drops around two volts, while other colors differ. This forward voltage is important because the resistor must drop the remaining supply voltage. A common beginner mistake is to connect an LED without a resistor directly between five volts and ground — this can draw too much current and potentially damage the LED, wires, or Arduino pin. Remember: resistors are not polarized, so they can face either way in the circuit, but LED orientation is critical for correct operation. LEDs: polarity and forward voltage means observe leg length for polarity and subtract the led forward voltage when computing resistor values; never omit the resistor.. In practical terms, why led orientation and voltage drop matter. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: LED rules
keyIdea.text: Observe leg length for polarity and subtract the LED forward voltage when computing resistor values; never omit the resistor.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.4 › LEDs
Definition

LED polarity and forward voltage

An LED only lights when current flows from anode to cathode. Forward voltage determines the voltage dropped by the LED when conducting.

Identify polarity
Long leg = anode (+), short leg = cathode (−). If uncertain, check datasheet or LED marking.
Forward voltage
Subtract forward voltage from supply to find the voltage the resistor must drop.
Scenario
If you connect a red LED backwards it simply won't light. If you omit the resistor, the LED and the Arduino pin may be exposed to excessive current. Always include a resistor in series and check LED orientation before powering the circuit.
Pro tip
If unsure which leg is which, bend the legs slightly and note the longer one for the anode; practice makes the identification quick.

screens.title: Breadboard anatomy
screens.subtitle: Understand power rails, rows, and the central groove

narration.text: A breadboard is a reusable prototyping board with a grid of holes connected by internal metal clips. Long holes along the edges are usually power rails: all holes on the same rail are connected, which is convenient for distributing five volts and ground. The central area is arranged in short rows of five holes where each row is connected internally. There is a central groove that separates the left and right halves; this gap lets you place integrated circuits so each pin connects to a separate row. When you insert a component leg into a row of five, it shares that connection with other inserted components in the same row. A frequent source of confusion is assuming columns or adjacent rows are connected across the groove; they are not. Use jumper wires to route signals between rows and to the Arduino pins. Before you wire a project, identify the rails and test continuity mentally by imagining which holes are electrically tied together. This mental check prevents common wiring mistakes when building your LED circuit. Breadboard anatomy means power rails run along the edges, rows of five are connected across the central area, and the mid groove separates the halves for ic placement.. content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.4 › Breadboard
Architecture

How the breadboard is wired

Recognize the power rails, the grouped five-hole rows, and the center groove so you can place parts and route connections without accidental shorts.

Power rails
Long columns along the edges commonly serve as +5V and ground; all holes in a rail are connected.
Middle rows
Rows of five holes are connected. Use them for single components and to chain connections with jumper wires.
Common error
Mistaking rows across the central groove as connected leads to wiring failures. The groove intentionally isolates the halves so ICs can straddle it.
Practical check
Before powering, trace one hole in a rail and one hole in a middle row and confirm they are part of the same group to build confidence in your layout.

screens.title: Placing components on the breadboard
screens.subtitle: Putting the LED and resistor where they belong

narration.text: When assembling the LED circuit, place the LED and resistor so current flows through the resistor into the LED to ground. Insert the LED so its anode connects to the Arduino pin through a jumper and the cathode connects to one side of the resistor; the other side of the resistor should go to ground rail. If you want the LED and resistor in series on the same row, use adjacent rows connected in a chain with a jumper spanning the necessary holes. Remember resistors can be placed either way because they are not polarized, but the LED must have the correct orientation. Use red jumper wire to connect the Arduino five-volt or signal pin, and black or blue for ground to keep wiring conventions clear. After wiring, visually confirm that the resistor is between the LED leg and ground and that no other parts form a direct short between five volts and ground. This step-by-step placement reduces error and makes troubleshooting straightforward. Placing components on the breadboard means always place the resistor in series with the led between the arduino pin and ground and follow color conventions for clear wiring.. In practical terms, putting the led and resistor where they belong. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Wiring pattern
keyIdea.text: Always place the resistor in series with the LED between the Arduino pin and ground and follow color conventions for clear wiring.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.4 › Component placement
Step-by-step
  1. Insert LED so anode and cathode occupy separate rows of five.
  2. Place resistor so one lead connects to the LED cathode row and the other to the ground rail.
  3. Use a jumper from Arduino pin 13 to the LED anode row.
  4. Use a ground jumper to connect the breadboard ground rail to Arduino GND.
  5. Verify no direct connection exists between 5V and GND rails before powering.
Example layout
LED anode → jumper to pin 13. LED cathode → resistor → ground rail → Arduino GND. This ensures current flows through resistor then LED to ground.
Troubleshoot
If the LED doesn't light, check polarity, ensure the resistor is in series, and confirm the ground rail is connected to Arduino GND.

screens.title: Step-by-step wiring: build the LED blink circuit
screens.subtitle: From parts to blinking LED with the Blink sketch

narration.text: Let's walk through building the classic LED blink circuit. Begin with the Arduino powered off. Insert the LED into the breadboard so its legs occupy separate rows. Place a 220-ohm resistor with one leg in the LED cathode row and the other leg in the ground rail. Use a jumper wire from Arduino pin 13 to the LED anode row; use a black jumper from the ground rail to Arduino GND. Double-check that the resistor is between LED cathode and ground and that the anode is connected only to the pin. Once wiring is confirmed, power the Arduino and upload the Blink sketch; the external LED should blink in sync with the onboard LED. If brightness seems high, swap the resistor for a larger value like 1k and observe the dimming. If the LED does not light at all, recheck polarity and that the ground rail is tied to Arduino GND. This controlled step-by-step approach reduces mistakes and helps you focus on one connection at a time. screens.title: Common mistakes and safety practices
screens.subtitle: Avoid shorts, check limits, and protect your Arduino

narration.text: Beginners often make a few recurring mistakes that are easy to avoid with simple checks. The most dangerous is creating a short by connecting five volts directly to ground without a load; this can damage power supplies and wires. Another frequent error is omitting the resistor when driving an LED, which allows excessive current to flow through the LED and the Arduino pin. Confusing breadboard rows across the central groove leads to wiring that looks correct but is electrically incorrect. To avoid these, always disconnect power before rearranging, follow color conventions so power and ground are obvious, and ensure every LED has a resistor. Also respect Arduino pin current limits by keeping individual pin currents low; when you need more power, use a transistor or dedicated driver. Before powering, do a quick visual check: are any jumper ends touching other rails? Is the ground rail connected to the Arduino GND? This safety-first habit prevents component failures and keeps your experiments repeatable. Common mistakes and safety practices means avoid shorts, always use a resistor with leds, verify ground connections, and keep pin currents within safe ranges.. Common mistakes
Short circuits
Directly connecting 5V to ground creates a short. Always check for accidental bridging before powering.
No resistor on LED

Incorrect breadboard rows

If in doubt
Choose a larger resistor to reduce current or double-check wiring; a slightly dim LED is safer than a burned component.

screens.title: Hands-on activity: LED blink and resistor swap
screens.subtitle: Build, run Blink, then observe effects of changing resistor values

narration.text: For the hands-on activity you will build the LED blink circuit and then experiment with resistor values to see how current affects brightness. Start with the Arduino disconnected from power and insert the LED and 220-ohm resistor as taught. Connect pin 13 to the LED anode and connect the resistor to ground, then attach Arduino GND to the breadboard ground. Power the board and upload the Blink sketch; confirm the external LED blinks. Next, power down, replace the 220-ohm resistor with a 1k resistor, and power up again. You will notice the LED becomes noticeably dimmer because the larger resistor limits current more. This controlled swap demonstrates the relationship between resistor size and current without changing code. As you perform this lab, record the perceived brightness and the resistor values used. This practice trains you to reason from calculation to observation, and reinforces the safety habit of powering down before changing wiring. The experiment also prepares you to select resistors when designing stronger or dimmer indicator circuits. screens.title: Quick assessment: current through a 330Ω resistor
screens.subtitle: Compute the current and explain why a resistor is required with an LED

narration.text: Here is a short calculation and explanation to check understanding. Suppose a resistor of 330 ohms is connected to a five-volt source. Using I equals V divided by R, the current is five volts divided by 330 ohms, which is approximately 0.0152 amps, or 15.2 milliamps. This simple arithmetic confirms that a 330-ohm resistor produces a safe LED current when used with a five-volt supply and a device drop accounted for. The reason a resistor is required with an LED is that the LED alone has a low dynamic resistance once it conducts. Without a resistor, the LED and Arduino pin would try to draw as much current as the source and wiring allow, which can exceed the safe current for the LED and the microcontroller pin and cause damage. Use the resistor to control current, keep the component within its safe operating region, and protect the Arduino. This reasoning is directly applicable when choosing resistor values for indicator LEDs and similar small loads. Quick assessment: current through a 330Ω resistor means i = 5 / 330 ≈ 15.2 ma. the resistor limits current so the led and arduino pin remain within safe operating limits.. In practical terms, compute the current and explain why a resistor is required with an led. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 2 › Chapter 1.4 › Assessment
Calculation
I = V / R = 5V / 330Ω ≈ 0.01515 A, or 15.2 mA. This is a practical LED current value when a forward drop has been accounted for.
Why use a resistor?
The resistor limits current so the LED and microcontroller pin do not exceed their safe current ratings. Without it a short-like condition can occur.
Explain in one sentence
A resistor is required to set the current through the LED to a level that both the LED and Arduino pin can safely handle.
Extension
Try calculating currents for different resistor values and note how that predicts brightness changes seen in the lab activity.

screens.title: Key Concepts — What to Remember
screens.subtitle: Three compact concept cards to anchor learning

narration.text: Let's recap the essential ideas you should carry forward. First, voltage, current, and resistance are linked by Ohm's Law; use V equals I times R and its rearrangements to compute currents or resistor values. Second, LEDs are polarized and have a forward voltage; always place a resistor in series to limit current and observe leg length for correct orientation. Third, breadboards have power rails along the edges and grouped rows of five separated by a central groove; verify rail and row connectivity before wiring. These three rules guide safe, predictable prototyping with Arduino. Carry a resistor calculator or do the quick arithmetic on paper when designing indicator circuits, always power down when changing wiring, and follow color conventions for power and ground to simplify troubleshooting. With these compact rules you can build small circuits confidently and avoid common beginner pitfalls.

narration.text: As a final quick reference, keep three one-line reminders by your workspace. First: voltage pushes, current flows, resistance limits — use Ohm's Law to compute what you need. Second: LED orientation matters and resistors are required in series to keep currents safe. Third: breadboard rails and five-hole rows determine connectivity — check them and tie ground to the Arduino before testing. These short reminders help you make quick decisions while wiring and testing. When in doubt, power down, measure or recalculate, and choose the larger resistor to err on the side of safety. With these compact rules you can move from blinking a single LED to adding sensors and other outputs with confidence.
